TI Public acceptance and attitudes toward procedures performed by medical
   students in Japan: a nationwide online survey
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Medical education; Clinical clerkship; Invasive procedures; Public
   attitudes; Japan
ID INTERPRETIVE SKILLS; EDUCATION; EXPERIENCES; CONSENT; SIMULATION
AB Background Clinical clerkships are essential in medical education, but ethical and legal restrictions limit the invasive procedures performed by medical students in Japan. The 2023 revision of the Medical Practitioners' Act permits students to conduct supervised procedures, such as venous blood collection and ultrasound examinations, after passing certain exams. This study investigates the public acceptance of these procedures, identifies barriers, and explores strategies to enhance medical student education patient-student collaboration.Methods A cross-sectional internet-based survey was conducted in Japan from April 4-6, 2023, targeting 3,771 participants aged 18-79, stratified by sex and age. The attitudes and consent toward the medical procedures performed by students were assessed using a seven-point scale and bipolar adjective items. Demographic and socioeconomic factors were investigated as covariates. Open-ended responses were analyzed qualitatively. Linear regression with covariate adjustments was performed using Stata SE version 16.Results Out of 3,771 participants, 37.8% were from the Kanto region, 59.9% were married, 56.7% had children, and 44.7% had at least a college-level education. Women generally held more negative views toward the attitudes and consent process of medical students performing abdominal ultrasound examinations. In contrast, elderly individuals (70-79 years) and homemakers had a more positive perception regarding blood collection. The primary reason for consent was contributing to medical education (93.2%), whereas the key reasons for declining consent involved students' skills (82.7%) and lack of trust (81.8%).Conclusion Older individuals and homemakers were more receptive toward procedures performed by medical students, particularly invasive ones. Addressing concerns about technical competence, privacy, and anxiety through improved communication, transparency, and supervised training can enhance patient acceptance and trust in medical education.

TI Factors influencing pharmacy program choice and career attitudes among
   Tanzanian tertiary students
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pharmacy education; Career choice; Professional attitudes; Tanzania;
   Pharmacy students; Cross-sectional study
AB Background While pharmacy education has expanded in Tanzania, students' motivations for choosing the profession and their career expectations remain underexplored. Understanding these drivers is crucial for aligning training with healthcare needs, enhancing professional satisfaction, and ensuring graduates contribute effectively to national health priorities. Methods A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted between March and July 2025 among 324 undergraduate pharmacy students conveniently sampled from St. John's University of Tanzania (SJUT), DECCA College of Health and Allied Science (DECOHAS), and Kampala International University of Tanzania (KIUT) in Tanzania. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analysed using STATA version 17. Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and multivariate logistic regression were employed to identify associations between factors influencing program choice and career attitudes, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. Results Pharmacy was the first-choice program for 76.2% of participants, and 53.7% demonstrated positive career attitudes (p = 0.01). Significant associations with selecting pharmacy as first choice were found for institution attended (chi & sup2;=13.587, p = 0.001), program level (chi & sup2;=13.862, p < 0.001), confidence in choice (chi & sup2;=7.438, p = 0.006), program reputation (chi & sup2;=14.75, p < 0.001), source of influence (chi & sup2;=14.742, p = 0.002), advice from pharmacists/healthcare workers (chi & sup2;=4.105, p = 0.043), and attitudinal disposition (chi & sup2;=7.342, p = 0.007). After adjustment, significant predictors of choosing pharmacy first included low confidence (AOR = 0.33, p = 0.046), program reputation (AOR = 0.39, p = 0.017), negative attitude (AOR = 0.54, p = 0.047), and community pharmacy career goals (AOR = 3.82, p = 0.045). Conclusion Pharmacy program choice among Tanzanian students is influenced by institutional factors, professional reputation, mentorship from healthcare professionals, and attitudinal disposition rather than financial incentives. Structured mentorship programs and enhanced career guidance are recommended to align student expectations with workforce needs.

TI Childcare challenges among surgical trainees and faculty: a
   single-institution study
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Childcare; Parenting; Residency; Faculty development; Career planning
AB Background Previous studies have demonstrated the challenges of parenthood in surgical training and careers. However, certain aspects of childrearing for surgeons remain understudied. We aim to leftacterize the complexity and costs of childcare amongst surgical trainees and faculty.Methods An anonymous, self-administered survey was conducted within the Department of Surgery at a large academic medical center. Both male and female trainees and faculty were included in the analysis. Chi-square or Fisher's Exact test was performed.Results Forty-six respondents provided information about childcare costs, with 37% of respondents being residents or fellows. Trainees worked longer workhours (p = 0.003) than their faculty counterparts. Despite trainees having fewer (p = 0.001) and younger (p = 0.001) children, there was no statistically significant difference in the annual childcare costs (p = 0.6). Over half of trainees and faculty report spending more than $20,000 annually. Childcare costs seem to place a greater burden on trainees, with 89% of trainees and 46% of faculty reporting that they are worried about the cost of childcare (p = 0.04). In addition to the expense, coordinating childcare is also challenging, with most respondents reporting multiple sources of childcare.Conclusion Concerted efforts are needed to support surgeon-parents at all career stages. The cost of childcare places an increased burden on surgical trainees compared to their faculty counterparts. Management of multiple sources of childcare is also a source of stress for both faculty and trainees.

TI VirtuScope: development of a high-fidelity virtual microscope simulation
   system for histology education
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Virtual microscope simulation; High-fidelity simulation; Computer
   graphics; Histology education; Medical laboratory training
AB Background Microscope operation is a core skill in morphological laboratory education. However, traditional instructional approaches often face limitations in equipment accessibility, procedural guidance, and hands-on opportunities. With the advancement of virtual simulation technologies, new pathways have emerged for improving practical skill training. This study presents the development of VirtuScope, a high-fidelity virtual microscope simulation system, and explores its application value in histology education. Methods VirtuScope was developed as a standalone virtual simulation system for microscopes, featuring 1:1 3D structural reconstruction and high-fidelity simulation of physical interactions and optics, powered by advanced human-computer interaction and computer graphics. Key simulation features include focus adjustment, objective switching, and light source control. In the instructional design, VirtuScope was integrated into a blended teaching model combining video guidance, self-directed practice, and progressive transition to real microscope use. Student feedback and learning outcomes were evaluated using pre- and post-course questionnaires and knowledge tests. Results Students rated the system highly in terms of image clarity, interactivity, and instructional support. Most participants reported improved understanding of microscope structure and operation, and over 90% expressed willingness to use VirtuScope in future learning. Knowledge test scores showed significant post-course improvement (p < 0.001), and the overall recommendation rate reached 98.52%. Conclusion VirtuScope demonstrates strong adaptability and educational support capacity. Its visual, interactive, and repeatable features enhance learning efficiency and practical competence, offering a scalable complement to traditional microscopy training. Moreover, it provides a feasible solution for institutions with limited laboratory resources, extending access to high-quality microscopy education across diverse learning environments.

TI Duke Cancer Care Experience: a longitudinal, multidisciplinary oncology
   curriculum for medical students
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Oncology Education; Medical School Curriculum; Multidisciplinary Cancer
   Care; Empathy Development
ID EMPATHY
AB Background Cancer prevalence continues to rise in the United States with a projected shortage of oncologists in the workforce. Despite this need, medical schools often lack oncology-focused education in their curriculum. Duke's Cancer Care Experience (CCE) is a multi-disciplinary elective designed to meet the growing demand for highly competent, compassionate, and diverse physicians of all medical specialties who are aware of the unique needs of patients diagnosed with cancer. CCE integrates principles of adult learning theory to increase learner engagement and prioritize knowledge retention of cancer care principles.Methods This single-group pre-post educational evaluation assessed first-year medical students enrolled in the Cancer Care Experience (CCE) using pre- and post-program electronic surveys administered via Qualtrics. Students in each cohort participated in workshops, lectures, case-based learning exercises, and longitudinal clinical shadowing experiences. Pre- and post-program surveys were administered to students, assessing career interests and self-efficacy within various aspects of oncology-related competencies, and completed an abbreviated IRI-derived empathy measure adapted from the AAMC Y2Q/GQ format. Participation was voluntary, and responses were anonymized. Data was collected from 2023-2025 to assess impacts over time.Results Among enrolled students, 36/40 (90%) in 2023 and 39/40 (98%) in 2024 completed both pre- and post-program surveys. Post-program mean comfort ratings were higher than pre-program ratings across all 15 surveyed cancer care topics in both cohorts, with absolute increases ranging from 15.90 to 41.95 points in 2023 and 11.03 to 34.06 points in 2024. On post-program evaluation, students rated the course highly for clerkship preparation, clinical shadowing, and breakout sessions, and many reported that the program influenced how they approached patients and their anticipated career choice. In a 2025 follow-up survey, 50.7% (36/71) of respondents reported anticipating a career in oncology, 74.6% (53/71) said CCE had influenced their thinking about career choice, and 98.6% (70/71) said they would recommend the course to other students.Conclusions Participation in the CCE was associated with higher post-program self-reported confidence across multiple evaluated cancer care domains. Respondents noted that the course played a role in shaping their understanding of oncology, and in some cases, their career interest. Although these findings should be interpreted as exploratory and descriptive given the single-group design and self-reported outcomes, the results still suggest that this model may serve as a scalable framework for integrating oncology education into pre-clinical medical curricula.

TI Integrating ChatGPT into nursing education: a randomized trial exploring
   knowledge, retention, and student perspectives on endotracheal
   suctioning
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; ChatGPT; Endotracheal suctioning; Knowledge
   retention; Nursing education
AB Aim This study aimed to evaluate the preliminary effectiveness of a ChatGPT-integrated educational session on nursing students' knowledge acquisition and retention regarding endotracheal suctioning, and to explore their perspectives and learning experiences. Methods A pilot pre-test/post-test parallel-group randomized controlled trial with an embedded qualitative component was conducted with 32 undergraduate nursing students who participated voluntarily. Participants were randomly assigned to either a ChatGPT-integrated education group or a traditional education group. Knowledge was assessed using a structured test administered before, immediately after, and six weeks following the intervention. Quantitative data were analyzed using appropriate non-parametric statistical tests, while qualitative data were analyzed thematically following Braun and Clarke's approach. Results While no significant difference was observed between groups in immediate post-test knowledge scores, the ChatGPT-integrated group demonstrated significantly higher knowledge retention over time at the six-week follow-up (p < 0.05). Qualitative findings revealed three main themes: learning supportive factors, student gains, and suggestions for improvement. Participants reported that interactive learning supported by ChatGPT facilitated active participation and reinforced learning. Conclusions The findings suggest that ChatGPT-integrated education has the potential to enhance knowledge retention over time, although it may not significantly impact immediate learning outcomes. Given small sample size, these result should be considered preliminary. Future large-scale studies are recommended to examine long-term outcomes and address potential implementation challenges.

TI "I learned more, but it was very hard:" advancing urban mathematics
   through blended learning, digital tools, and modeling in an

LA English
DT Article
DE blended learning; digital tools; mathematical modeling; technology
   integration; urban education
ID ACHIEVEMENT; TEACHERS; REFORM; IMPACT
AB Historically marginalized students attending urban schools often experience teacher-directed, lecture-based, and memorization-focused mathematics instruction, contributing to disengagement and disinterest in mathematics fields. Technology integrated mathematics instruction holds promise to advance engagement and increase levels of cognitive demand; however, little is known about high school students' perceptions of such innovations. This study examined an engineering-embedded algebra elective class designed to integrate blended learning, digital tools, and modeling-based problem solving in two urban high schools. Findings suggest that aligning technology integration with instructional design, teacher roles, and educational context can enhance student engagement and, as a result, potentially support algebraic understanding. This exploratory study highlights the potential of technology-rich, modeling-centered curricula to expand access to rigorous mathematics learning in urban education settings.

TI From co-design to co-adaptation: the evolution of teacher professional
   learning across a long-term research practice partnership
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE co-adaptation; co-design; computational thinking; next generation
   science standards; professional learning; research practice partnership;
   science education; stem
ID COLLABORATIVE DESIGN; SCIENCE CURRICULUM; CONTEXT; IMPLEMENTATION;
   COHERENCE; MODEL
AB This paper presents an intrinsic single case study of a Research Practice Partnership (RPP) focused on helping teachers learn to integrate computational thinking and sensor-based physical computing into inquiry-oriented middle school science and STEM instruction aligned with the Next Generation Science Standards. Over the six-year partnership, 32 teachers participated and 49 professional learning (PL) workshops. This paper draws on an extensive dataset including PL field notes, analytic memos, team meeting notes, and interviews with school district administrators that was analyzed using inductive, interpretive and descriptive approaches. This case study suggests that it is both plausible and important to shift PL structures and activities over time within an RPP, such as moving from co-design to co-adaptation, and offers insights into the rationale and dynamics of such a shift.

DT Article

   personal assistant
AB Introduction As AI-powered learning assistants become increasingly integrated into higher education, understanding their pedagogical impact across different technological designs is crucial. This study investigated the impact of a mobile chatbot learning assistant in a first-year university course, with attention to both its overall educational contribution and the effects of evolving chatbot technology.Methods This quasi-experimental, multi-cohort study followed five iterations of a first-year university course over a five-year period. Nevertheless, students evaluated the chatbots positively, particularly in terms of usability, accessibility, and support outside regular school hours. Compared with the decision tree-based version, the LLM-driven chatbot showed a modest advantage in promoting engagement and offering more personalized support.Discussion Although chatbot integration did not lead to measurable gains in academic achievement, it was perceived as a valuable supplementary learning tool. The results suggest that AI chatbots may contribute more strongly to student experience and perceived support than to direct performance outcomes. In addition, the slight benefits of the LLM-driven version suggest that advances in chatbot design may enhance engagement and personalization in educational settings.

AB University education encourages the development of rigorous scientific research, making it essential to improve redaction skills. TI Collective wellbeing in action: educator-informed architecture for
   community flourishing
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE educator wellbeing; community development; culturally-sustaining
   education; educational leadership; mixed-methods research;
   organisational change; schoolwide wellbeing
ID MENTAL-HEALTH; TEACHER; PERSPECTIVE; DECADE
AB Beyond an international trend or policy myopia, wellbeing occupies a prominent position across educational, governmental, and intergovernmental agendas as a strategic investment generating workforce, and societal returns including educator retention, student outcomes, and institutional effectiveness. In educational environments, dynamic relationships among stakeholders create living ecosystems wherein flourishing emerges from - and simultaneously sustains - the vitality of educators, learners, families, and communities. Recently, intergovernmental educational policy has directed wellbeing attention to the workforce at its heart - educators themselves. Rather than framing teacher and leader wellbeing as a deficit to be remedied, this mixed methods study revealed pathways for enhancing individual and collective wellbeing for early childhood, primary, and secondary educators across Aotearoa New Zealand through an appreciative, transformative, and culturally-affirming lens. An explanatory sequential mixed methods design framed this research as an integrated inquiry: a national cross-sector survey of 735 educators provided statistical breadth, while 10 semi-structured interviews captured depth and complexity. Orienting this interdisciplinary research at the juxtaposition of education, health, psychology, sociology, and organisational scholarship supported the generation of original findings that address research gaps while offering pragmatic frameworks for change. Therefore, theoretical and conceptual anchors for this piece include appreciative inquiry, complexity thinking, positive education, asset-based community development, and indigenous worldviews. Findings revealed educator wellbeing practices as fundamentally relational, paradoxical, complex, and contingent upon organisational and systemic conditions. Contributions to the field include a holistic conceptualisation of wellbeing, empirical findings, and a framework. Rather than prescriptive universal solutions, the framework, An Architecture for Community Flourishing, offers compass-like principles enabling multi-level, context-responsive implementation within and potentially beyond educational settings. This paper proposes that collective wellbeing, operationalised through regenerative responsibility across individual, relational, organisational, and systemic dimensions, offers pathways for community flourishing to emerge.

   methods; project-based learning

TI Translanguaging as a metacognitive scaffold strategy: reframing EFL
   instruction
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE EFL instruction; English-only approach; Latin America; learners'
   autonomy; metacognition; multilingual education policy; policies;
   reframing
AB Metacognitive regulation-specifically planning, monitoring, and evaluation-is essential for effective foreign language learning. However, English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instruction in Latin America rarely leverages learners' linguistic repertoires to support higher-order processes. Translanguaging may serve as a potential scaffold for metacognitive engagement, but its cognitive mechanisms and pedagogical implications remain relatively under-theorized in regional EFL scholarship. This perspective article examines two guiding questions: (1) How can translanguaging function as a metacognitive strategy that enhances learners' planning, monitoring, and evaluation processes? (2) What contextual, pedagogical, and policy-related factors influence the positioning of translanguaging as a metacognitive strategy in Latin American EFL classrooms, and what instructional patterns emerge from this analysis? Drawing on research published between 2015 and 2025, the article integrates sociocultural and metacognitive theory to propose a conceptual reframing in which translanguaging may function as a deliberate regulatory tool that can support learners in externalizing thinking, comparing meanings, and evaluating understanding. The analysis highlights insights and empirical evidence regarding vocabulary retention, reading comprehension, collaborative knowledge construction, and leaners' autonomy. The analysis also suggests the presence of policy-level ambiguities regarding the role of learners' linguistic repertoires in EFL instruction. Based on this analysis, the paper proposes pathways for practice, including bilingual learning objectives, prewriting in L1, translanguaging circles, and scaffolded content language integrated learning (CLIL) approaches. This article argues for rethinking EFL pedagogy through a metacognitive lens and calls for policy frameworks that acknowledge learners' full linguistic repertoires as resources for language learning.

SO EDUCATION IN THE KNOWLEDGE SOCIETY
LA Spanish
DT Article

   technology
ID SOCIAL NETWORKS
AB Digital competence is a recurring theme in educational research, especially in recent years, due to scientific and social advances, as well as changes in educational regulations and teacher training processes in this area. However, the number of studies focused on digital competence in primary education students is limited. Consequently, this study focuses on evaluating the perceptions of third-cycle Primary Education students regarding their digital competence. TI Factor structure of an Arabic version of the Five-Facet Mindfulness
   Questionnaire
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Arabic validation; confirmatory factor analysis; Five-Facet Mindfulness
   Questionnaire; mindfulness; psychometric properties
ID 5 FACET MINDFULNESS; PSYCHOMETRIC PROPERTIES; SELF-REPORT; VALIDATION;
   VALIDITY; FFMQ
AB Mindfulness refers to an individual's ability to pay attention to present experiences with openness and awareness. The Five-Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ) assesses five components: Observing, Describing, Acting with Awareness, Non-Judging, and Non-Reactivity. This study examined the factor structure an Arabic version of the 39-item FFMQ among two independent samples of university students (n = 570 and n = 456). Five structural models were tested: single-factor, correlated four-factor, hierarchical four-factor, correlated five-factor, and hierarchical five-factor. The findings indicated a poor fit for the single-factor model, but a good fit for both the correlated four- and five-factor models. The correlated four-factor model-excluding the Observing facet-demonstrated the most parsimonious and robust fit. Values of Cronbach's alpha as an estimate of reliability were good reflecting the internal consistency among the items of each facet. This study recommended that researchers and practitioners can use the Arabic FFMQ for assessing mindfulness in Arabic-speaking populations with non-mediating experiences.

ID ENGAGEMENT
AB The objective of this study was to comparatively analyze university students' perceptions of hybrid learning in Ecuador using a questionnaire previously validated in Greece. TI Spaces that 'hold' us, spaces that 'stretch' us: a transdisciplinary
   study into positive learning experiences in South Africa
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE arts-based methods; emotional wellbeing; experience impact; learning
   experience; learning space; South Africa; transdisciplinary
AB This paper investigates how spatial conditions affect learning experiences in Africa. The qualitative study asked postgraduate students and lecturers to share recollections of how everyday learning spaces affected their learning, to discover meaningful and transformational experiences. The transdisciplinary group of participants represented Architecture, Education and Theology. The research is situated in South Africa, an example of low- and middle-income countries. Structural inequalities and resource constraints are evident in limited school and classroom infrastructure, negatively impacting the quality of education for the majority of South Africans. Participants were asked to write retrospective letters as a participatory-inspired arts-based method. Inductive data analysis revealed various types of learning spaces, their conditions, and associated learning experiences. It was found that the abstraction of certain spatial conditions encourages interactive pedagogy despite physical limitations, resulting in learning experiences that can 'hold' and 'stretch' students. Meaningful and transformational experiences emerged in spaces that 'hold' and spaces that 'stretch', in which students feel safe before they can grow and develop. Spaces that 'hold' can occur in inadequate learning conditions, but in which students feel valued, comfortable and emotionally safe. Spaces that 'stretch' prompt students to express freely, exercise their agency, be challenged to develop personal identities and foster meaningful relationships with other people and with nature. Various learning spaces and conditions enable positive experiences, but are not innovative learning environments, nor are they custom-designed. Instead, they are everyday learning spaces that are the norm in a local South African school.

TI Beyond named methods: A typology of active learning based on classroom
   observation networks
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID INTRODUCTORY PHYSICS; SCIENCE; STUDENTS; LECTURE
AB A growing number of introductory physics instructors are implementing active learning methods in their classrooms, and they are modifying these methods to fit their local instructional contexts. However, we lack a detailed framework for describing the range of what these instructor adaptations of active learning methods look like in practice. Existing studies apply structured protocols to classroom observations and report descriptive statistics (e.g., the fraction of class time spent on each activity), but this approach overlooks the complex nature of instruction. In this study, we apply network analysis techniques to classroom observations to define a typology of active learning that considers the temporal and interactional nature of instructional practices. We analyze video data from 30 instructors at 27 institutions who implemented one of the following named active learning methods in their introductory physics or astronomy courses: Investigative Science Learning Environment (ISLE), Peer Instruction, Tutorials, and Student-Centered Active Learning Environment with Upside-down Pedagogies (SCALEUP). We first create one classroom observation network per instructor that captures temporal sequences of activities measured using the Classroom Observation Protocol for Undergraduate STEM (COPUS). We then calculate the cosine similarity between all pairs of observation networks, create a similarity network where each instructor's classroom observation network is a node and the edges represent cosine similarity, and apply the Infomap clustering algorithm to the similarity network to identify types of active learning instruction. We find five types of instruction: clicker lecture, dialogic clicker lecture, dialogic lecture with short groupwork activities, short groupwork activities, and long groupwork activities. We find no significant relationship between these instruction types and the named active learning methods; instead, implementations of each of the four methods are spread across different instruction types. This result prompts a shift in the way we discuss and study active learning: the names of developed active learning methods may not actually reflect classroom instruction. We also find that student conceptual learning does not vary across the identified instruction types, suggesting that instructors may be flexible in the style in which they implement these methods without sacrificing effectiveness. We discuss the implications of these results for both research and the professional development of college physics instructors.

TI Exploring the Effects of Virtual and Physical Escape Rooms in Pharmacy
   Ethics and Legislation
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Educational escape room; Pharmacy education; Active learning;
   Gamification; Virtual learning
AB Objective: To develop and evaluate both physical and virtual educational escape rooms (VER) for teaching ethics and legislation in pharmacy and to assess their impact on knowledge and perceptions among third-year student pharmacists. Methods: A quasi-experimental intervention study was conducted in which the physical and VER were designed around 4 stations based on various acts and regulations in pharmacy. They were implemented during tutorial sessions across 2 cohorts of third-year student pharmacists, 2023/2024 and 2024/2025. Pre- and postknowledge assessments on ethics and legislation were used to measure the effectiveness of the intervention. A 12-item questionnaire captured participants' perceptions, along with demographic data and prior escape room experience. No notable differences in perceptions were observed between the 2 formats. Gender-related differences in learning concentration under stress were noted, but prior experience with escape rooms did not affect perceptions. Conclusion: Educational escape rooms, whether physical or virtual, are effective tools for enhancing student pharmacists' knowledge of ethics and legislation and fostering positive learning perceptions. The virtual format may offer added benefits for knowledge retention.

TI Evaluating the Longitudinal Integration of a Medication Safety Training
   Program into a PharmD Curriculum
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pharmacy education; Student pharmacist; Medication safety; Community
   engagement; Prevention education
AB Objective: To describe the longitudinal integration of a virtual medication safety training program (Ambassadors) into a PharmD curriculum and evaluate its impact on knowledge retention, Ambassador self-efficacy, and Ambassador self-intentions as students apply their training in both curricular and cocurricular experiences. Methods: First-year PharmD Students completed the Generation Rx Ambassador training program as a requirement in their Concepts in Patient Care course. Students applied their Ambassador training in their first year through both required [small group workshop and community introductory pharmacy practice experiences] and optional (medication safety outreach event) practice activities. Knowledge gains, Ambassador self-efficacy, and Ambassador self-intentions were evaluated utilizing pre-, post-, and 6-month post-surveys. A qualitative thematic analysis evaluated the incorporation of medication safety messaging into experiential rotations. Results: Students demonstrated statistically significant knowledge retention and gains in Ambassador self-efficacy from pre-to post-and 6-month post-surveys. Ambassador self-intention decreased significantly from post-to 6-month post-surveys. A sub-analysis showed that the small group workshop significantly impacted self-intention, and students who participated in the optional outreach event reported statistically significant increases in both self-efficacy and self-intention. Findings from the thematic analysis indicated that most students felt confident during patient interactions within their community introductory pharmacy practice experience and felt that their conversations about medication safety were positive, supporting increased self-efficacy. Conclusion: Longitudinal integration of a medication safety training program (Ambassadors) and practice application activities into a PharmD curriculum was a successful method to increase student knowledge and self-efficacy in delivering medication safety messaging.

TI Virtual reality and simulation for the teaching of sterile
   pharmaceutical manufacturing in pharmacy education: A cross-sectional
   evaluation of student opinions
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Virtual reality; Simulation; Pharmaceutical compounding; Pharmacy
   education; Pharmacy students
AB Introduction: Use of virtual reality (VR) is increasing in education. A VR and simulation field trip was developed, allowing students to experience a walkthrough of a sterile pharmaceutical manufacture site using three modalities: a VR headset with 3D static tour, 2D static desktop tour and a 360 degrees dynamic video tour. This study aims to understand student opinions, assess usability of the modalities used and investigate potential for a simulation to replace physical site visits. Methods: Data from undergraduate pharmacy and postgraduate pharmaceutical science students was gathered through an online survey. A system usability scale (SUS) score was calculated for each modality. Responses were coded and analysed using descriptive and inferential statistics and open-text responses were analysed using conventional content analysis. Results: Data was collected from 82.3% (n = 79) of students who participated in the virtual field trip. Most students (97.4%, n = 76) across both courses were either extremely satisfied or satisfied with the session. Almost two thirds of students (64.9%, n = 50) ranked VR walkthrough highest, followed by 360 degrees video walkthrough (19.5%, n = 15) and desktop walkthrough (15.6%, n = 12). Two out of three students (66.7%, n = 12) with previous on-site experience agreed the virtual field trip could replace a physical site visit. Open-text responses revealed advantages and drawbacks versus physical visits. All modalities displayed acceptable usability. Most students (91.0%, n = 71) would welcome wider use of VR and simulation in their course. Conclusion: Positive results obtained highlight potential for greater implementation of VR and simulation to support teaching of sterile manufacturing and increase student accessibility to manufacturing sites.

TI Community Clubs: needs assessment and efficacy of a school career
   development program
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic achievement; academic skills; career development; consultation;
   secondary education; social-emotional skills
ID ADOLESCENTS; STUDENTS
AB Introduction School-based career interventions have shown consistent effectiveness in supporting students' developmental tasks and future planning. Current approaches emphasize a holistic perspective of career development, integrating personal and social development, educational achievement, and career management competencies. Although policy frameworks recognize the importance of these domains, structural challenges such as school-to-work transition difficulties and persistent youth unemployment highlight the need for preventive and developmentally oriented interventions. The present article reports two complementary studies: Study 1 explores adolescents' social-emotional skills and career adaptability to inform the implementation of the intervention, while Study 2 evaluates the effectiveness of a career consultation program targeting these skills among 10th-grade students.Method Study 1 used a convenience sample of 155 students (58.7% girls; M age = 15.47, SD = .86). Study 2 followed a quasi-experimental design with an intervention group (n = 73; 71.2% girls; M age = 15.51, SD = .87) and a comparison group (n = 67; 52.2% girls; M age = 15.24, SD = .68). In Study 1, students completed a sociodemographic questionnaire and measures of social-emotional skills, career adaptability, and digital literacy, at a single time point in 2021. In Study 2, students completed the same measures, along with instruments assessing career exploration, school engagement, and study processes, at pre-test and post-test, during the 2021-2022 school year. In Study 2, no statistically significant improvements were observed within the intervention group regarding social-emotional skills and career adaptability. Nevertheless, post-test comparisons showed between-group differences in some social-emotional skills, career exploration, school engagement, study processes, and grades.Discussion Although effects emerged more clearly in secondary outcomes than in the core target competencies, findings highlight the value of systematically evaluating career interventions and the relevance of context-sensitive, developmental practices within school psychology services.

TI Beyond fluency: perceived professional growth across repeated simulation
   cycles in scientific english for psychology
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE empathy; linguistic skills; professional communication; scientific
   English; simulation-based learning
AB Simulation-based learning is increasingly used in higher education to connect language learning with professionally oriented communication, yet less is known about how students perceive their development across repeated simulation cycles in discipline-specific English settings. This longitudinal mixed-methods study examined perceived development among 81 first-year undergraduate students enrolled in a Scientific English module within the Psychology degree program. Students participated in two simulation cycles focused mainly on self-harm and addictions and completed the same ad hoc questionnaire after each cycle. The instrument assessed two dimensions, Perceptions and Emotional Engagement (PEE) and Professional Competence and Communication (PCC), and included open-ended questions. Quantitative findings showed significant increases from the first to the second simulation in total scores, PEE, and PCC, with stronger gains in professional competence and communication. Qualitative findings indicated that these changes were associated with greater confidence, a more applied understanding of empathy, improved management of emotionally and ethically complex situations, and increased confidence in professionally oriented communication in English. Students also identified repetition, realism, collaboration, and preparation as key supports for learning. Overall, the findings suggest that repeated simulation can support more reflective, confident, and professionally oriented participation in discipline-specific English settings while fostering early professional awareness among psychology students.

TI Governing education for sustainable development in low- and
   middle-income countries: normative convergence and operational
   divergence in global education governance
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Global education governance; Education for Sustainable Development
   (ESD); Multiagency governance architecture; Education policy coherence;
   Low-and middleincome countries
AB Education for Sustainable Development has become an instrument through which international organizations shape national responses to accelerating socio-ecological crises, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. This paper presents a theory-driven comparative analysis of three global frameworks shaping ESD governance: UNESCO's Education for Sustainable Development for 2030 Roadmap, the UNFCCC's Action for Climate Empowerment and the Education 2030: Incheon Declaration and Framework for Action. The paper conceptualizes these frameworks as an interacting global governance field rather than isolated policy instruments. It argues that divergences in governance logic, institutional design, and operational expectations structure how sustainability commitments are interpreted and enacted. Drawing on qualitative document analysis, the study finds that while the three frameworks converge normatively, they diverge sharply in pedagogical orientation, accountability mechanisms, and assumptions about national institutional and professional capacity. With ESD 2030 emphasizing pedagogical transformation, ACE embedding education within climate governance, and the Incheon FFA situating ESD within broader education reform, distinct and partially misaligned implementation expectations emerge. These divergences generate implementation challenges related to policy coherence, teacher capacity, assessment, and knowledge integration. The study contributes to debates on global education governance by explaining why global consensus on ESD does not translate into coherent national reform pathways, particularly in low- and middle-income contexts.

TI Does flipped classroom improve students' evaluations of teaching
   quality?
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Flipped classroom; Students' evaluation of teaching; Higher education;
   Students' engagement; Econometrics
ID COGNITIVE LOAD; ACHIEVEMENT; SATISFACTION; ENGAGEMENT; SEEQ
AB This study investigates the impact of the Flipped Classroom (FC) model on the multidimensional evaluations of teaching quality in an undergraduate econometrics course. Grounded in Student Engagement and Cognitive Load theories, the research examines how a shift to the FC model influences distinct teaching dimensions. TI Developing citizenship competencies in accounting students through
   experiential learning: An action research study
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Experiential learning; Action research; Citizenship; Accounting
   education; Responsible leadership
AB Calls for more socially responsible professionals underscore the need for accounting graduates to possess citizenship competencies for meaningful engagement with diverse stakeholders in an increasingly globally connected business landscape. Few studies explore pedagogical approaches to develop such competencies in accounting students, especially in complex post-colonial contexts. Addressing this gap, this study explores how community-based experiential learning can be optimised to develop citizenship competencies. Action research was employed across two cycles of an experiential learning programme at a South African university, designed using Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory and framed by Pless, Maak and Stahl's model for responsible leadership development. A triangulated dataset comprising reflections and peer- and selfevaluations, supported by questionnaires, were analysed using thematic analysis, descriptive statistics, and non-parametric statistical tests. The action research approach facilitated iterative refinements, to which strengthened perceptions of competency development between cycles were likely attributable. Based on these findings, the study provides empirically grounded recommendations for community-based citizenship development, including academic transcript recognition, rubric-based assessments, and scaffolded, structured reflections. Experiential designs should incorporate sustained engagement through repeat visits, enabling participants to observe the tangible impact of their involvement and thereby fostering greater social responsibility. Intentional experiential exposure to unfamiliar community contexts, including diverse cultural and socio-economic backgrounds, enhances a broad spectrum of citizenship competencies, notably empathy and social awareness, but also extending to tolerance and adaptive communication skills. The insights from this study support professional programme development that seeks to deliver socially responsible graduates who can contribute to the public interest beyond technical expertise.

TI Turning intent into practice: Operationalising sustainability Co-design
   in business schools
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Co-design; Governance; Sustainability; Curriculum; Engagement;
   Assessment; Southeast Asia
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; KEY COMPETENCES; FRAMEWORK
AB This paper examines how a governance-aware co-design model can turn institutional sustainability intent into scalable, practice-centred learning and assessment in a Southeast Asian Business School. Using a practice-led mixed-methods design, we identify participation drivers and frictions through surveys and focus groups embedded in a short modular intervention. Practical implications include embedding engagement indicators and feedback loops into programme review, accreditation, and performance compacts. The contribution is a pragmatic blueprint for institutionalising co-design, so sustainability learning remains legible, auditable, and scalable in resource-constrained contexts.

TI Network analysis of perceived barriers to evidence-based practice
   teaching among nursing clinical mentors: A cross-sectional study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Evidence-based practice teaching; Network analysis; Nursing clinical
   mentors; Nursing education; Teaching barriers
ID EDUCATION
AB Background: Nursing clinical mentors play a crucial role in developing evidence-based practice (EBP) competencies among nursing students. However, the implementation of EBP teaching remains challenging. Aim: To identify and compare core barriers to EBP teaching among nursing clinical mentors using network analysis. Design: Cross-sectional study. Setting(s): Four university-affiliated tertiary hospitals in China. Participants: A total of 715 nursing clinical mentors participated in the survey. Methods: A 28-item EBP teaching barriers scale was used to assess perceived barriers. Network analysis was conducted to identify central and bridge nodes. Subgroup comparisons were performed across diffusion stages. Results: Perceived barrier levels were moderate to high, with scores declining as participants advanced through diffusion stages. The three most severe barriers were lack of expert nursing discussion (A2), lack of time for new ideas at work (O2), and lack of time to read research (O1). Network analysis identified the strongest edge between lack of support from non-physician staff (O7), and administrative restrictions (O8) (edge weight = 0.790). Notably, centrality analysis revealed a clear discrepancy: barriers perceived as most severe (A2, O2, O1) were not the most central. Instead, O7, O8, and lack of practical validation (I6) emerged as the most central nodes (strength = 14.377, 14.348, and 14.260, respectively). I6 also served as a key bridge node. Although the overall network structures showed no statistically significant differences across stages (Stage 1 versus Stage 2: p = 0.406; total sample versus Stage 1: p = 1.000; total sample versus Stage 2: p = 0.535), distinct patterns of central and bridging nodes emerged. Conclusions: This network analysis reveals an interconnected barrier system where organizational and evidence-translation challenges are central, while traditional high severity barriers like time constraints are less influential. The observed mismatch between perceived severity and network centrality suggests the potential value of more targeted strategies. Network-informed interventions focusing on central barriers and tailored to diffusion stages may enhance the implementation of EBP teaching among nursing clinical mentors.

TI Salary and teacher retention across the performance distribution
SO ECONOMICS OF EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Pay for performance; Career path; Teacher salaries; Teacher retention;
   Eco-nomics of Education
ID STUDENT-ACHIEVEMENT; PAY; INCENTIVES; TURNOVER; SCHOOLS
AB Retention of effective teachers has significant implications for student outcomes. Thus, un-derstanding factors that influence teacher retention is a central concern in education research. I use a performance pay scheme to study the relationship between salary and teacher decisions to exit or become an assistant principal along the performance distribution of teachers. Applying a regression discontinuity design, I find that teachers whose salary can increase across the cutoff are 4.2 percentage points less likely to exit the district public school system when they score just above the cutoff, even in the absence of dismissal threats. I find no statistically significant effect for teachers with no financial incentive around the cutoff. Exploring heterogeneity in teacher responses across the performance distribution yields suggestive evidence that high-performing teachers are less responsive to salary. While low-performing teachers, who are subject to additional performance requirements to advance in the salary schedule, are more likely to exit when they face no financial incentive and score just above the cutoff. I find suggestive evidence that performance burdens can be as effective as dismissal threats in incentivizing attrition, but only among low-performing teachers with competitive outside options.

AB Using the conservation of resources theory, this study aimed to examine how and when perceived flu/cold severity influenced teachers' well-being. TI Instructional and cognitive interventions improve undergraduates'
   critical thinking via distinct neurocognitive mechanisms
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Critical thinking; Instructional intervention; Cognitive intervention;
   Metacognition
ID DISPOSITIONS; SKILLS; INTELLIGENCE; OSCILLATIONS
AB Background: Critical thinking, the ability to reason analytically, evaluate evidence and resist cognitive bias, has become increasingly essential as students navigate information-rich environments. However, evidence on interventions that promote critical thinking and reveal their neurocognitive mechanisms remains limited. Aims: This study examined how metacognitive instructional and adaptive cognitive training interventions affect students' critical thinking and whether they engage distinct neurocognitive patterns. Sample: Participants were 74 undergraduate students majoring in science and engineering. Methods: A 3 & times; 2 mixed pretest-posttest design was employed. Participants were randomly assigned to instructional, cognitive, or control groups. The intervention groups received four weeks of intervention, while the control group received none. Behavioral assessments were conducted at baseline, immediately after the intervention, and at a six-month follow-up. Electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded at baseline and posttest during belief-bias syllogistic reasoning to capture neural changes related to the interventions. Results: Both interventions led to significant improvements in critical thinking, which were maintained over a sixmonth follow-up. However, their neural oscillatory patterns diverged: the instructional intervention increased frontocentral beta and decreased parietal alpha power, reflecting enhanced metacognitive regulation and analytical reasoning, whereas the cognitive intervention reduced frontocentral theta and parietal alpha activity, indicating improved processing efficiency and access to working memory. Implications: The study reveals the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying critical thinking enhancement and underscores the importance of integrating diverse, evidence-based approaches into higher education to cultivate enduring and transferable reasoning skills.

AB High-stakes tests play a decisive role in test-takers' lives and in shaping educational policies, yet they are often criticized for encouraging rote learning and limiting higher-order cognitive engagement. This study aimed to analyze the underlying cognitive processes measured in the domain-specific content knowledge section of the National PhD Entrance Exam (NPEE) in Teaching English as a Foreign Language (TEFL) in Iran, a high-stakes exam with far-reaching consequences. Employing a mixed-methods design, the quantitative phase analyzed item responses from 1000 examinees using the cognitive diagnostic model G-DINA, which was integrated with Bloom's taxonomy of cognitive learning to investigate the underlying cognitive skills required to answer test items and provide a comprehensive understanding of the low- and higher-order cognitive levels of test-takers. In the qualitative phase, semi-structured interviews were conducted with PhD students and university professors from different universities. Results revealed that the test failed to measure cognitive skills beyond the executing level, corresponding to the third level of Bloom's taxonomy. Findings further indicated that test items relied predominantly on recall of theories and factual details, creating a mismatch between the skills assessed and those required for TEFL PhD program real-life tasks. Stakeholder interviews emphasized that the exam underrepresents essential postgraduate competencies such as research ability, critical thinking, and problem solving. These shortcomings may result in negative washback effects by fostering teaching to the test, and undermining the quality of postgraduate TEFL research as well as deep learning in tertiary-level education.

TI Undergraduate chemistry students' sensemaking in a laboratory setting:
   the interplay of knowledge gaps and epistemic emotions
SO CHEMISTRY EDUCATION RESEARCH AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
ID COGNITIVE LOAD; SENSE
AB This study investigates how undergraduate chemistry students engage in sensemaking during an inquiry-based Boyle's law laboratory activity, focusing on how different types of knowledge gaps and associated epistemic emotions guide their sensemaking trajectories. A holistic multiple-case study design was employed, with sensemaking episodes serving as the unit of analysis. Two student groups were purposefully selected to represent contrasting sensemaking trajectories. Group 1 exhibited a sustained sensemaking trajectory and completed the activity, whereas Group 2 exhibited a disengaging sensemaking trajectory and ultimately withdrew from the task without arriving at a coherent resolution. Data were collected through audio and video recordings, activity sheets, and epistemic emotion diaries, and were analyzed thematically. The results revealed clear differences between the groups. Group 1 primarily encountered procedural knowledge gaps. These gaps involved relatively low element interactivity and were resolved through collaborative reasoning. By contrast, Group 2 encountered conceptual and epistemic gaps that required the coordination of multiple abstract constructs, imposed high cognitive demands, and remained unresolved. Epistemic emotions also diverged markedly across the two groups. Both began the activity with curiosity and surprise, yet Group 1 sustained positive emotions that helped them manage confusion productively. Group 2 experienced increasing frustration and boredom, reflecting a trajectory of hopeless confusion that hindered sustained sensemaking. The interaction of unresolved gaps and negative epistemic emotions seemed to be associated with Group 2's disengagement. The findings suggest the instructional relevance of attending to both cognitive demands and epistemic emotions, particularly in moments when students encounter persistent knowledge gaps during laboratory sensemaking.

TI Learner Satisfaction with Technical and Non-Technical Skills in an
   Accredited Healthcare Simulation Centre: A Retrospective Study
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE clinical simulation; professional competence; health personnel attitudes
ID CRITICALLY-ILL PATIENTS; RESUSCITATION; PERFORMANCE
AB Clinical simulation is a cornerstone of healthcare education, yet comparative evidence on learner perceptions of technical skills (TS) versus non-technical skills (NTS) training remains limited. This study aimed to examine Kirkpatrick Level 1 satisfaction across simulation course types and explore associations with participant characteristics. We conducted a retrospective analysis of 1806 healthcare professionals who attended 133 simulation sessions between 2024 and 2025. Participants completed a 16-item ad hoc questionnaire (Cronbach alpha = 0.959) covering four domains scored 1-10. Domain scores were compared between TS (n = 1224) and NTS (n = 582) courses using Welch t-tests and Cohen's d. Spearman correlations assessed associations with age, gender, and professional category. Overall learner satisfaction was excellent (mean 9.55 +/- 0.70). TS courses scored significantly higher across all domains (p < 0.001), with effect sizes ranging from small (d = 0.21-0.28) to moderate-approaching (d = 0.45) in the Simulation/Methodology domain. Item-level analysis highlighted perceived improvement in technical skills (d = 0.49) and error awareness (d = 0.43) as the most discriminating factors. Age, gender, and professional category were significantly associated with course type (all p <= 0.020). Both TS and NTS simulations achieve high learner satisfaction. The perceptual advantage of TS courses suggests that instructional strategies enhancing the tangibility of NTS learning outcomes are warranted to optimize learner engagement and satisfaction.

TI An Exploratory Cross-National Study of K-12 Teachers' Generative AI
   Literacy and Classroom Enactment
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE generative AI; K-12 teachers; cross-country comparison; AI literacy;
   teacher professional development
AB Guided by Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), this qualitative study examines how K-12 teachers across five countries, the United States (n = 7), India (n = 5), Qatar (n = 5), Colombia (n = 5), and the Philippines (n = 4), conceptualize AI literacy and integrate generative AI into their practice. Through 26 semi-structured interviews conducted in summer and fall 2025, we identified three cross-national patterns that challenge dominant narratives about AI adoption in education. First, institutional support did not uniformly predict AI literacy depth: the four Filipino teachers developed sophisticated prompt engineering competencies despite low institutional backing, while the five Indian teachers showed the lowest awareness despite strong organizational support. Second, prompt engineering awareness functioned as a critical differentiator between teachers who engaged with AI as a pedagogical skill and those who treated it as an opaque productivity tool. Third, AI use for lesson preparation far outpaced classroom-facing application across all contexts. These findings reframe AI readiness as a question not of access and support but of whether conditions cultivate the interaction competence that meaningful integration demands.

TI When using entrustable professional activities thwarts basic
   psychological needs: A case study of residents' experience
SO MEDICAL TEACHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Assessment; internal medicine; competency-based education; postgraduate
   medical education
ID SELF-DETERMINATION THEORY; MEDICAL-EDUCATION; COMPETENCE; MOTIVATION;
   EPAS; AUTONOMY; TIME
AB Background: Entrustable professional activities (EPAs) were introduced to link competencies with clinical work and support residents' professional and competence development. Yet their implementation has raised concerns about burdensome documentation and limited educational value. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory (SDT), we examined how residents experienced EPAs in relation to their needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness-needs essential for optimal motivation and professional development. Methods: We conducted an instrumental case study in a Canadian internal medicine residency program. Fourteen residents participated in semi-structured interviews. We used Braun and Clarke's six-phase thematic analysis, with SDT guiding our interpretation of how participants' narratives reflected their experiences of autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Results: Residents experienced EPAs as compliance exercises disconnected from meaningful professional development. Four interrelated themes captured how these experiences related to residents' basic psychological needs: (1) A Documentation Imperative demonstrated how external pressures to accumulate observation forms constrained residents' autonomy and discouraged formative use of feedback, undermining competence; (2) Fleeting Convergences captured how EPAs and competence development operated on largely separate trajectories, with only occasional moments of alignment; (3) Electronic Barriers highlighted how documentation platforms replaced feedback dialogue with impersonal transactions, weakening relatedness while reducing opportunities for autonomous engagement and understanding performance gaps, if any; and (4) A Binding Burden showed that shared bureaucratic struggles fostered peer solidarity among participants, though this relatedness centered on coping rather than collaborative learning. Conclusions: Current use of EPAs often fails to support the conditions necessary for meaningful engagement with EPAs and, in some cases, actively thwarts them. Documentation burdens constrained autonomy, competence was weakly supported, and relatedness was strained by transactional processes-a drift from EPAs as professional activities to fragmented assessment tasks. Addressing these challenges is essential if EPAs are to function as intended: units of professional practice to be entrusted to residents.

TI Building confidence in music performance: a teacher-led self-efficacy
   approach
SO MUSIC EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Music education; performance; anxiety; self-efficacy; psychological
   skills
ID STATE ANXIETY; MENTAL SKILLS; STUDENTS; PROGRAM
AB Self-efficacy is a strong predictor of achievement and a key factor in wellbeing. Yet, few interventions have targeted this construct in music performance or been designed for adolescent students. A 14-week, teacher-guided programme based on an educational model of performance self-efficacy which included psychological skills training, simulation and self-evaluation, was embedded into adolescent studio and class lessons. A pilot study followed by two main studies, one within a class (intervention n = 47; control n = 25) and the other in a studio (intervention n = 24; control n = 7) music lesson setting supported the utility of this approach. Self-efficacy was significantly enhanced for intervention participants. This was associated with improvements in anxiety, psychological performance skills, and self-, teacher-, and independently-evaluated music performance. Differential treatment effects in the timing, range and magnitude of the effects were also observed for the two instruction conditions. These results provide support for the educational model offering a practical method for developing key skills essential to success and wellbeing.

TI "Falling through the cracks": parents' perceptions of a dyslexia
   diagnosis and support in Australian primary schools
SO AUSTRALIAN JOURNAL OF LEARNING DIFFICULTIES
LA English
DT Article
ID DEVELOPMENTAL DYSLEXIA; CHILDREN; PERSPECTIVES; IRELAND; MOTHERS; IMPACT
AB This study investigates Australian parents' experiences with identification and support of primary school-aged children diagnosed with dyslexia. From the parent perspective, it evaluates whether recent government initiatives intended to support dyslexic students are perceived as positively impacting these students. Data collection included online surveys and semi-structured interviews, analysed using frequency distribution tables and thematic analysis. The findings reveal many parents identified children's reading difficulties early on but were dissatisfied with the support provided by schools and the high costs and long wait times for diagnosis. Parents expressed concerns that evidence-based reading instruction and adequate accommodations were not implemented, even when included in IEPs, which parents attributed to a lack of teacher knowledge and training regarding dyslexia and support strategies. This research highlights specific experiences of students with dyslexia falling through the cracks and the urgent need for systemic changes in the Australian educational framework to better support these students.

TI A Lecture-Specific AI-Based Tutor for Higher Education: Pedagogical
   Design and Empirical Evaluation
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE generative AI; chatbot; higher education; intelligent tutoring system;
   learning analytics; constructivist pedagogy; educational technology
ID PREDICTIVE-VALIDITY; FAILURE; POINT; ITEM
AB Generative AI tools are increasingly used in higher education, yet most available systems lack pedagogical grounding, course alignment, and insight into student learning. This paper presents the development, implementation, and evaluation of the bioTutor, an open-source, course-specific AI chatbot designed to support constructivist learning in large university classrooms. The system integrates a curated knowledge base, a didactically structured interaction design, and a learning analytics dashboard for instructors that summarizes anonymized student-chatbot conversations. To assess students' perceptions of usefulness, ease of use, learning relevance, output quality, and result demonstrability, we developed an education-adapted extension of the Technology Acceptance Model (edTAM) and applied it in an introductory biology course with 407 enrolled students. During a 23-week deployment, students generated more than 10,000 interactions across over 1000 conversations. Questionnaire data indicate high usability, strong perceived usefulness, and broad interest in adopting similar tools. Usage patterns show that the bioTutor was employed both for learning and exam preparation. These findings suggest that students perceived pedagogically structured, course-grounded AI chatbots as useful for learning and exam preparation, while the lecturer dashboard provided aggregated insights into students' questions and recurring difficulties. The open-source framework enables adaptation to other disciplines and provides a scalable foundation for further research on didactically informed AI systems in higher education.

TI The associations between prejudices, motivation, and Attitude Towards
   inclusion of future special needs teachers
SO EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Special needs; teachers; prejudices towards disability; motivation;
   attitude towards inclusion
ID BEHAVIOR RELATION; SELF-REGULATION; ORGANIZATION; EDUCATION; SENTIMENTS
AB To enhance the educational experience of all students, the attitudes of special education teachers towards inclusion play a pivotal role. Within this framework, pre-service training programs should encourage critical reflection on personal beliefs, potential biases, and motivational orientations. The present study aimed to examine the relationships among these variables in a sample of 355 pre-service teachers aged between 19 and 59 years (M = 37.40; SD = 8.24). Findings indicated significant negative association between prejudices towards individuals with special needs and the other variables under investigation, whereas a positive association emerged between autonomous motivation to become a special education teacher and attitudes towards inclusion. These results emphasise the relevance of considering individual characteristics in the preparation of future special education teachers.

TI Addressing Basic Psychological Needs in a Pre-Scientific Initiation
   Program in Chemistry: A Triangulated Analysis in Light of
   Self-Determination Theory
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE High School; Research in Chemical Education; Inquiry-Based Learning;
   Pre-Scientific Initiation
AB Motivation to learn chemistry depends not only on cognitive factors but also on the satisfaction of basic psychological needs, as proposed by the Self-Determination Theory (SDT). Despite evidence on the motivational role of inquiry practices, there are still gaps to be filled when it comes to understanding how Prescientific Initiation Programs meet these needs in basic education. This study investigated how participation in a Prescientific Initiation Program, linked to a Chemistry department, contributes to the satisfaction of autonomy, competence, and relatedness (bonding) among high school students, in light of the SDT. The study was carried out using a convergent mixed-methods design approach; the approach involved the conduct of 13 interviews with students, 5 interviews with supervising teachers, and a questionnaire administered to 15 students, analyzed using the Basic Psychological Needs at Work Scale (BPNWS) database. The interviews were examined by using content analysis, and the quantitative data collected were treated by using descriptive statistics. The results suggest high perceived satisfaction with autonomy (mean = 4.38) and competence (mean = 4.40), reinforced by reports of freedom of choice, responsibility, and the development of scientific skills. Relatedness presented greater variability (M = 3.87), reflecting differences in the consistency of the social support. The findings indicate that participants perceived the program as supporting self-determined motivation, engagement, and strengthening of scientific identity. The study suggests the implementation of practices and actions geared toward improving social integration and encouraging the expansion of similar programs in chemistry education. Future research should employ larger sample sizes and longitudinal analyses in order to obtain more comprehensive results.

   Hydrogen Evolution: A Comprehensive Laboratory Experiment for
   Undergraduates
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article

   Compounds; Nanoconfined Effect; Hands-OnExperience; Material Science
ID MESOPOROUS SILICA
AB With the continuous rapid development of materials science, integrating innovative synthesis strategies into undergraduate experimental courses is crucial for bridging fundamental knowledge with cutting-edge research. This study proposes a comprehensive experimental scheme for undergraduates, focusing on the solid-phase synthesis of ultrafine intermetallic compounds within a mesoporous carbon matrix. TI Providing a Structured Support System and Mentoring Facilitates the
   Transformative Power of Education for Currently and Formerly
   Incarcerated Persons
SO URBAN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Currently and formerly incarcerated people (CIP & FIP); prison
   education; reentry; mentoring
AB Within 5 years of prison release, 46% of individuals return to prison. Participating in correctional educational programming while incarcerated reduces 1-year reincarceration rates by 28% when compared to those that do not participate. While education is a powerful protective factor, many incarcerated populations lack access to systems of support that enable higher educational pursuits. Using data from 540 currently and formerly incarcerated prison-to-professional (P2P) scholars applicants, we investigated the influence of structured support and peer mentoring services on educational and employment outcomes. P2P scholars outperformed non-P2P and non-formerly incarcerated students across matriculation rates, employment rate, persistence, grade point averages, and recidivism.

TI Microscopic matters and multispecies pedagogies: Re-creating
   professionalism in early childhood education
SO CONTEMPORARY ISSUES IN EARLY CHILDHOOD
LA English
DT Article
DE dust; early childhood; environmental education; multispecies
   ethnography; posthumanism; professionalism
AB The global climate crisis demands a transformative shift in environmental education that foster relational engagements with multispecies and the wider ecological world. This transformation requires an expansion of notions of 'professionalism' and justice, calling for new knowledges and urgent actions to address the devastating consequences of anthropogenic activity on planetary ecologies. In response, this paper proposes alternative conceptions of professionalism that move beyond humanist thought and individualised educational frameworks. Engaging with the microscopic matter of dust, this study explores how the agency of dust and child-earth relations can reconfigure understandings of professionalism through mapping and microscope encounters. Dust is approached as an agentic material entangled with children's bodies, technologies and ecological systems, revealing connections between professionalism, capitalism, colonialism, pollution and creative ecological microworlds. Situated in a kindergarten in Melbourne, Australia, the research applies multispecies ethnography to disrupt dominant child-centred paradigms and hierarchical separations between humans and the rest of the world. This paper contributes to the re-creation of professionalism by recognising the pedagogical significance of multispecies, material and sensory engagements. It invites educators to move beyond exclusive human agency and toward co-constructed knowledge and experience with multiple others. The study offers implications for early childhood pedagogies that are ethical, speculative and ecologically attuned, foregrounding the need for professionalisms-to-come that be responsive to planetary futures.

TI A Method for Monitoring SEL Implementation in the Classroom
SO CONTEMPORARY SCHOOL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
ID DRUG-ABUSE PREVENTION; QUALITY IMPLEMENTATION; STUDENT OUTCOMES;
   PROGRAM; SCIENCE; INTERVENTIONS; ADOLESCENTS; UNIVERSAL; FRAMEWORK;
   MATTERS
AB Planning for, monitoring, and evaluating social and emotional learning (SEL) program implementation can be as important to student outcomes as program selection, yet it is often overlooked in research and practice. SEL implementation data can be used to enhance both implementation and outcomes and guide ongoing monitoring and future implementations. Evaluation of implementation activities enables practitioners to make more informed decisions about program selection and use, assess program effectiveness, evaluate cultural and contextual relevance, and determine the sufficiency of training and technical support. The development of the Social Emotional Learning Tracking Tool (SELIT) was informed by original research and a synthesis of SEL implementation theory and research. The SELIT uses a multi-faceted approach to program and strategy implementation. The SELIT addresses a gap in the literature by offering researchers and practitioners a program-independent method to guide dimensions of implementation such as adaptations, dosage, adher-ence, quality, and student engagement.

TI Student Professional Collaboration as a Contemporary Format for
   Knowledge Sharing and Conducting Research in the University Environment
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE professional collaboration; teacher-education students; cooperative
   learning
ID PEER ASSESSMENT; SCIENCE
AB This study aimed to describe the profile of professional collaboration among students in teacher-education programmes and to examine whether readiness for further collaboration is associated with prior experience. The work was conducted within a university grant of Abai Kazakh National Pedagogical University and implemented as a descriptive-comparative study based on a posttest cross-sectional snapshot with no baseline measurement. Data were collected via Google Forms from 91 students of the Department of Primary Education (Years 1-4). The questionnaire covered collaboration experience (yes/no), frequency of participation in joint projects, perceived value of collaboration (1-5), perceived impact on the learning experience, readiness to participate in joint research/projects in the future (1-5), and open-ended questions on motivations, barriers, and expected university support. Prior collaboration experience was reported by 40.7% of respondents; participation was predominantly irregular (48.4% "never", 44.0% "rarely"). Perceived value was high (M = 4.05, SD = 1.15; Me = 4), and most respondents reported a positive contribution to their learning experience (75.8%). Readiness for future participation was moderately high (levels 4-5: 52.7%). A Mann-Whitney test indicated higher readiness among students with prior collaboration experience (U = 1288, p = 0.016, r = 0.29). Thematic grouping of open-ended responses showed that knowledge sharing and mutual support were the dominant motivations, while organisational/time and communication barriers were most frequently mentioned; the most commonly requested support measures included regular joint events and support for student communities. Findings are interpreted as a descriptive snapshot rather than causal evidence. The results may inform the design of facilitated collaboration formats and subsequent monitoring of student readiness.
